Every time I have extra cash, I buy more Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM). I have stopped apologizing for it. My thesis fits in one sentence. Within five years, TSMC will work like a utility for global computing: a toll road that AI accelerators, smartphone processors and data center chips have to use, and it pays shareholders for every trip.

Courtesy of Intel
Why Every AI Player Pays the Toll

On the third-quarter call, management said it plainly: "all the AI players are working with TSMC." Chips at 7nm and below made up 79% of wafer revenue. Production at 2nm grew from 3% of wafer revenue in Q2 to 8% in Q3. High-performance computing now brings in 68% of revenue. The company also says "demand is still far above our capability to supply today." I look for exactly that in a utility: a broad customer base (534 customers and 12,682 products in 2025) that keeps asking for more capacity than the company can build.

Receipts Behind My Buying

Start with growth. Third-quarter revenue reached $46.72 billion, up 41.2% YoY in USD terms. Management raised its full-year 2026 outlook to around 44% growth. Its Q4 guidance of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion works out to 58% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.

Next comes profitability. Gross margin came in at 66.4%, operating margin at 58.7% and ROE at 45.5%. EPS per ADR of $4.60 beat the $4.46 consensus.

The quarterly dividend rose from NT$6.00 to NT$7.00, and management says it is committed to a "sustainable and steadily increasing cash dividend per share." Can Healthy Revenue Growth Boost T-Mobile's Q3 Earnings?

T-Mobile US, Inc. TMUS is set to report third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 28, after the closing bell. It pulled off a trailing four-quarter earnings surprise of 17.3% on average, beating estimates on all previous occasions.

The wireless service provider is expected to witness year-over-year revenue growth, driven by subscriber additions, higher broadband adoption and strong demand for wireless services. However, higher promotional spending, intense competition and rising operating costs might have weighed on overall performance.

Factors at Play

During the quarter, T-Mobile strengthened its customer acquisition strategy by eliminating upfront costs for eligible customers, addressing a major barrier to switching wireless providers. The initiative is expected to have supported third-quarter 2026 revenues by attracting new subscribers, encouraging carrier switching and increasing adoption of its wireless plans.

T-Mobile's "Get iPhone 18 Pro on Us" promotion is likely to have contributed to revenue growth in the quarter under review. The offer might have attracted new customers, encouraged existing subscribers to upgrade their devices and increased demand for postpaid plans, boosting subscriber additions and recurring service revenues.

During the to-be-reported quarter, T-Mobile also promoted the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and Samsung's new Galaxy foldable smartphones through attractive device offers. These promotions might have encouraged smartphone upgrades, attracted new wireless customers and increased device sales across its retail and online channels.

Despite these growth opportunities, T-Mobile's September earnings could have been affected by higher promotional spending, device subsidies and customer acquisition costs amid strong competition. Continued investments in 5G networks and broadband expansion might also have increased operating expenses and depreciation, limiting profitability.

For the September quarter, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for total revenues is pegged at $23.31 billion, indicating an improvement from the year-ago quarter's reported figure of $21.96 billion. The consensus estimate for adjusted earnings per share is pegged at $2.86, implying growth from $2.59 reported a year ago.

Earnings Whispers

Our proven model does not conclusively predict an earnings beat for T-Mobile for the third quarter. The combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold) increases the chances of an earnings beat. However, that is not the case here.
